# Reminder Calendar (T = move date)

**Assumption:** Today is May 7, so I set **T ≈ Thursday, July 16, 2026** (10 weeks out). If your date differs, shift everything by the same amount. Two calendar notes: Memorial Day (May 25) and July 4 weekend both fall in this window, so offices close and movers and truck rentals get tight. Summer is also peak moving season, so book early.

**Correction to my earlier checklist:** Phase 1 says to send landlord notice right away, while Phase 3 says weeks 6-4. Check your lease and send notice by whichever deadline is earlier. Also, Oregon DEQ emissions testing applies to the Portland and Medford areas. I listed Klamath Falls earlier, and I don't believe it applies, so verify on the DEQ site.

## Now (T-10 weeks, ≈ May 7-13)
- **Check lease notice deadline** (J): Send written notice now if the lease requires 60+ days.
- **Request 3-4 mover quotes** (J): Verify each USDOT number on FMCSA SAFER; ask for video estimates.
- **Price truck and container options** (J): Compare U-Haul, Penske, PODS, and U-Pack against the mover quotes.
- **Book dog vet check-up** (M): Request all records, microchip number, and a travel-anxiety discussion.

## T-9 weeks (≈ May 14)
- **Decide movers vs. DIY vs. hybrid** (J): Compare total cost, including your time and fuel.
- **Decide drive vs. ship the car** (J): Get 2-3 shipping quotes if shipping.
- **Start Oregon housing search or confirm closing date** (M): Lock this in by T-8 if you can.
- **Ask employer about relocation help or remote work** (P): Get answers in writing.

## T-8 weeks (≈ May 21)
- **Sign Oregon lease or confirm closing** (J): Save copies to your "Move" folder.
- **Book mover or truck, and pay deposit** (J): Confirm valuation coverage (Full Value Protection) before paying.
- **Book vehicle shipping or reserve the driving route** (M): Peak-season slots fill fast.
- **Book temporary housing for the first 1-2 weeks** (J): Confirm that it's dog-friendly and note the pet fee.
- **Schedule Oregon internet install** (J): Request the earliest slot; installs can run 2+ weeks out.

## T-7 weeks (≈ May 28)
- **Book dog-friendly lodging for every night on the road** (M): Confirm each pet policy and fee in writing.
- **Start declutter in garage, storage, and closets** (J): Sort into keep, sell, donate, trash.
- **Schedule car maintenance** (M): Oil, tires, brakes, battery, and A/C, since summer heat is hard on cars.
- **Test dog on a 30-minute drive** (M): Note drooling, panting, or whining and tell the vet.
- **Open a "Move" folder, physical and digital** (P): Start collecting documents.

## T-6 weeks (≈ June 4)
- **Find an Oregon vet and ask for records transfer** (M): Book a visit for a few days after arrival.
- **Check Ohio title and lien status** (M): If there's a loan, call the lienholder about title requirements.
- **Research Oregon DMV steps** (M): Confirm the license and registration deadline (about 30 days) and whether you need a DEQ test.
- **Order packing supplies** (J): Boxes, tape, paper, wardrobe boxes, and markers.
- **List items to sell** (P): Post larger pieces now; they take longest to sell.

## T-5 weeks (≈ June 11)
- **Tell your employer your final move date** (P): Confirm last day, payroll address changes, and reimbursement paperwork.
- **Start packing non-essentials** (J): Decor, books, off-season clothes, guest room.
- **Get Oregon utility start dates in writing** (M): Electric, gas, water, trash.
- **Review travel plan with dog's vet if needed** (M): Get any calming meds or motion-sickness medication now.

## T-4 weeks (≈ June 18)
- **Send landlord or realtor final notice, if not already sent** (J): Request move-out inspection and deposit return address.
- **Schedule Ohio utility shutoffs for T+1 day** (J): Keep a day of overlap in case of delays.
- **Schedule donation pickups** (J): Many charities book 2-3 weeks out.
- **Call auto insurer about the move** (M): Confirm Oregon coverage start date and any rate change.
- **Request prescription refills** (J): Ask for a 30-90 day supply to cover the transition.

## T-3 weeks (≈ June 25)
- **Confirm mover or truck details** (J): Arrival window, crew size, payment method, final written estimate.
- **Order dog ID tag with a new phone number or temp address** (M): It arrives in time for the trip.
- **Pack most of the house** (J): Leave kitchen basics, daily clothes, and bathroom items.
- **Arrange dog care for moving day** (M): Sitter, boarding, or a friend's house away from the movers.
- **Notify banks, credit cards, and insurers of the address change** (J): Set the effective date for moving day.

## T-2 weeks (≈ July 2, with July 4 weekend ahead)
- **File USPS change of address** (J): Set the start date for moving day or the day after.
- **Confirm shipping pickup details** (M): Date, location, driver phone, and personal items removed.
- **Cancel or transfer subscriptions and memberships** (J): Gym, streaming, lawn service, meal kits; see the services timeline.
- **Confirm temporary housing and hotel reservations** (M): Reconfirm dates and dog policies before the holiday weekend.
- **Sell or donate remaining large items** (J): Last call for anything that isn't coming.

## T-1 week (≈ July 9)
- **Finish packing everything except essentials** (J): Label boxes by room with contents on the side.
- **Pack the "first night" box and moving day kit** (J): Include chargers, toiletries, bedding, tools, and dog supplies.
- **Defrost the freezer and clear out the fridge** (J): Use up or donate perishables.
- **Photograph valuables and record serial numbers** (J): Back up to the cloud.
- **Pack dog travel kit** (M): Food, water, bowls, meds, records, bed, toys, leash, waste bags.
- **Confirm Ohio shutoffs and Oregon start dates** (M): Make a final call on both ends.
- **Service the car and fill up** (M): Check tires and pack the emergency kit.

## T-2 days (≈ July 14)
- **Do the final cleaning pass** (J): Before the movers load, if you can; touch-ups after.
- **Confirm mover or truck arrival time** (J): Text or call to verify.
- **Charge all devices and download offline maps** (P): Mountain passes can have no signal.

## T-1 day (≈ July 15)
- **Get cash for tips and small expenses** (P): Typically $20-$50 per mover for a full-day crew.
- **Walk through the house with a checklist** (J): Closets, cabinets, attic, garage, and outdoor spaces.
- **Keep the documents folder with you** (J): Not in the truck.

## T = Moving day (≈ July 16)
- **Photograph every room before leaving** (J): Document the condition for the deposit.
- **Read the Bill of Lading before signing** (J): Never sign blank forms; keep your copy.
- **Photograph final meter readings** (J): Electric, gas, and water.
- **Secure the dog away from the loading** (M): Crate or a closed room with water and a familiar bed.
- **Return keys, remotes, and fobs; get a receipt** (J): Confirm where the deposit gets sent.
- **Start driving early** (M): Take breaks every 2-3 hours and never leave the dog in a parked car.

## After arrival
- **T+1 day: Photograph the new place and report damage** (J): Send it to the landlord in writing.
- **T+1 day: Confirm utilities and internet work; find shutoffs** (J): Water, breaker box, gas.
- **T+1 day: Start renter's insurance** (J): Make sure it's active from the day you get keys.
- **T+2 to T+7: Inspect delivered items against the inventory** (J): Note damage in writing right away. Don't wait.
- **T+3 days: First Oregon vet visit** (M): Transfer records and update the microchip address.
- **T+1 week: Update voter registration status and mail forwarding** (J): Confirm at sos.oregon.gov.
- **T+2 weeks: Oregon driver's license** (both): Don't wait until day 30.
- **T+2 weeks: Register vehicle(s) in Oregon** (M): Bring title, insurance, and any DEQ certificate.
- **T+2 weeks: Get the Oregon dog license** (M): County or city, depending on where you live.
- **T+30 days: Hard deadline check** (J): License and registration should be done.
- **After registration: Cancel Ohio plates and registration** (M): Confirm that nothing's left open.

---

# Room-by-Room Packing Checklist

**Timeline rule of thumb:** Start with the rooms you use least, and pack the kitchen and bathroom last. For a 1-2 bedroom home, expect roughly 20-40 hours of total packing time, plus extra if you're also decluttering.

## Kitchen (pack last; allow 4-6 hrs)
- [ ] Keep out: 1 pot, 1 pan, 2 plates, bowls, cups, utensils, a knife, a can opener, and coffee supplies
- [ ] Wrap plates vertically and pack them in small boxes; use dish-pack boxes for glassware
- [ ] Use towels and dish cloths as padding
- [ ] Toss expired pantry items; donate unopened non-perishables
- [ ] Don't pack open liquids, aerosols, or cleaning chemicals (most movers refuse them)
- [ ] Label: "Kitchen, fragile" and "Kitchen, heavy"

## Living room (2-3 hrs)
- [ ] Wrap art and mirrors, and use picture boxes
- [ ] Photograph the electronics wiring before unplugging
- [ ] Label cables with tape or bags
- [ ] Pack books in small boxes only, because they get heavy quickly
- [ ] Remove lamp shades and pack them separately

## Bedrooms (3-4 hrs each)
- [ ] Use wardrobe boxes for hanging clothes
- [ ] Keep a week's clothes and bedding for the road and the first night
- [ ] Disassemble bed frames and bag the hardware, taped to the frame
- [ ] Vacuum-bag off-season clothes and linens
- [ ] Pack jewelry and valuables yourself; carry them with you

## Bathrooms (1-2 hrs)
- [ ] Use a toiletry bag for the essentials
- [ ] Seal liquids in plastic bags
- [ ] Toss expired medications and cosmetics
- [ ] Carry prescriptions with you, never in the truck
- [ ] Pack towels last

## Home office (2-3 hrs)
- [ ] Back up all computers to the cloud and an external drive
- [ ] Carry laptops, hard drives, and important documents with you
- [ ] Shred what you don't need to keep
- [ ] Photograph the monitor and printer setup

## Garage, storage, and outdoor (3-6 hrs)
- [ ] Drain gas and oil from mowers and tools; movers won't take fuel
- [ ] Dispose of paint, propane, and chemicals through local hazardous waste
- [ ] Decide what's worth moving: cheap tools and old yard items often cost more to ship than to replace
- [ ] Bag the hardware from anything you take apart

## Closets and linens (1-2 hrs)
- [ ] Donate anything you haven't worn in a year
- [ ] Use linens as padding for fragile items
- [ ] Keep a set of sheets and towels for each person in the first-night box

## Dog items
- [ ] Pack a separate dog bag that rides in the car: food, bowls, meds, records, leash, waste bags, bed, toys
- [ ] Keep the crate out until the very last moment
- [ ] Don't pack the dog's bed or favorite toy in the truck

## "Open First" box (per room)
- [ ] Box cutter, scissors, tape, trash bags
- [ ] Toilet paper, soap, hand towels, paper towels
- [ ] Sheets, pillows, phone chargers
- [ ] Basic tools, light bulbs, and a flashlight
- [ ] Coffee maker, snacks, paper plates

---

# Declutter Tips

1. **Do it by category, not by room.** Clothes, books, kitchen, and papers go faster when you tackle them together.
2. **Use the cost test.** Movers charge by weight or space, and a $40 item costs more than that to move 2,400 miles.
3. **Sort into four piles:** keep, sell, donate, trash. Anything you can't decide on after 30 seconds goes in a "maybe" box with a date. If you haven't opened it by T-2 weeks, let it go.
4. **Sell early.** List big furniture by T-6 weeks. Anything unsold by T-2 weeks gets donated.
5. **Think about the Oregon space.** Measure your new rooms and check that large furniture fits through the doors.
6. **Ask what you'd buy again.** If you wouldn't repurchase it today, it probably doesn't need to ride across the country.
7. **Don't declutter sentimental items last.** Do them mid-way, when you're not exhausted.
8. **Schedule donation pickups early.** Many charities book 2-3 weeks out in summer.
9. **Digitize papers.** Scan what you can, and shred the rest.
10. **Keep a "leaving" corner** by the door, so donation boxes are already staged.

---

# Dog Checklist and Services Timeline

**Correction first:** Earlier I said a Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (CVI) is only needed if you fly. That was too simple. Many states technically require a CVI or health certificate for dogs entering by car, though it's rarely checked. Ask your vet, and check the Oregon Department of Agriculture's pet import page. If one is required, it's usually valid for about 30 days, so time it close to departure. (T = Thursday, July 16, 2026.)

---

# Consolidated Dog Checklist

## T-10 to T-8 weeks: Health and planning
- [ ] **M** Book the vet check-up (check-up, vaccines, heartworm and flea/tick prevention up to date). *(HIGH)*
- [ ] **M** Request full records: rabies certificate, vaccine history, microchip number, medication list, and any surgery or condition notes. *(HIGH)*
- [ ] **M** Ask the vet whether a CVI is needed for Oregon, and when to schedule it.
- [ ] **M** Discuss travel anxiety, motion sickness, and heat tolerance. Ask about anti-nausea or calming medication and **trial any new medication before the trip**, not on the road.
- [ ] **M** Decide drive vs. fly for the dog (see the flying section). Driving is usually less stressful for a dog.
- [ ] **M** Confirm the microchip is registered and the contact info is current.

## T-8 to T-5 weeks: Booking and conditioning
- [ ] **M** Book dog-friendly lodging for every road night. Get each pet policy and fee in writing. *(HIGH)*
- [ ] **M** Confirm the temporary Oregon housing allows dogs. Check breed or size limits and the pet deposit.
- [ ] **M** Buy a crash-tested harness or a well-secured, ventilated crate for the car. *(MED, $40–$200)*
- [ ] **M** Do crate or harness practice and 30-minute test drives, building to 1–2 hours.
- [ ] **M** Identify emergency vets along the route and near the destination. Save the numbers.
- [ ] **M** Find an Oregon vet and ask for a records transfer. Book a visit for T+3 days or so.
- [ ] **M** Look up your Oregon county or city dog license rules. Most require proof of rabies vaccination.
- [ ] **M** Check your new rental's pet policy: pet rent, deposit, and any documentation required.

## T-4 to T-2 weeks: Prep
- [ ] **M** Order a new ID tag with your new phone number and, if possible, a destination address. *(MED)*
- [ ] **M** Arrange dog care for loading day: sitter, boarding, or a friend's home. *(HIGH)*
- [ ] **M** Get a 30-day extra supply of medications and preventatives.
- [ ] **M** Get the CVI if needed, timed to the vet's guidance.
- [ ] **M** Take a clear current photo of the dog (for lost-pet posters, just in case).
- [ ] **M** Reconfirm all lodging dog policies before the July 4 weekend.

## T-1 week: Packing the dog kit (rides in the car, never the truck)
- [ ] Food for the trip plus 1 week extra, in a sealed container. Keep the same brand to avoid stomach upset.
- [ ] Water jug (bring water from home at first, then mix in new water gradually if your dog is sensitive)
- [ ] Collapsible bowls, leash, backup leash, harness
- [ ] Waste bags, paper towels, enzyme cleaner, and old towels (for accidents or car sickness)
- [ ] Medications, preventatives, and calming aids
- [ ] Records folder: rabies certificate, vet contact, CVI, microchip number
- [ ] Bed or blanket and favorite toys, with an unwashed item that smells like home
- [ ] Crate, with a cover or sunshade for the car windows
- [ ] First-aid basics: gauze, vet wrap, tweezers (ticks), and your vet's after-hours number
- [ ] Chews or a stuffed toy for hotel evenings

## Moving day
- [ ] **M** Dog is with the sitter, or in a closed room or crate with a "DO NOT OPEN" sign on the door.
- [ ] **M** Light meal the morning of travel, not a heavy one. Walk and exercise before getting in the car.
- [ ] **M** Collar, tag, and leash on the dog before any door opens.
- [ ] **M** Never leave the dog in a parked car, even for a few minutes. In July, interior temperatures can become dangerous within minutes.
- [ ] **M** Plan a break every 2–3 hours for water and a walk. Check pavement temperature with your hand, since hot asphalt burns paws.
- [ ] **M** Drive early or late in the day to avoid the worst heat through the Plains and Mountain West.

## Overnight arrangements
- [ ] Ask for a ground-floor room near an exit, if possible.
- [ ] Call ahead to confirm the pet policy, since some chains vary by location.
- [ ] Don't leave the dog alone in a room unless the hotel allows it. If you do, crate them and put out a "dog in room" sign.
- [ ] Bring the crate in for the night so the dog has a familiar space.
- [ ] Walk the dog before bed and first thing in the morning.
- [ ] Keep a towel to wipe paws and a sheet to cover hotel bedding if needed.

## Arrival and first two weeks
- [ ] **M** Set up a quiet "safe room" first with bed, water, and familiar items. Do it before the movers bring furniture.
- [ ] **M** Check the yard and fences for gaps. Walk the perimeter before letting the dog off leash.
- [ ] **M** Keep the dog on a leash for the first few days in unfamiliar territory.
- [ ] **M** Keep feeding and walking times as routine as possible.
- [ ] **M** Update the microchip registry with the new address. *(HIGH)*
- [ ] **M** Get the Oregon dog license. *(HIGH)*
- [ ] **M** First Oregon vet visit, with records transferred. *(HIGH)*
- [ ] **M** Look up local leash laws, dog parks, and any rental restrictions.
- [ ] **M** Watch for signs of stress (not eating, hiding, accidents). Call the vet if it lasts more than a few days.

---

# Pet-Fee Ballpark Costs

Fees vary widely and change often. Treat these as planning numbers and confirm with each property.

| Lodging type | Typical pet fee | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Mainstream hotels | $0–$100 per stay, or $25–$75 per night | Some chains charge per night, some per stay. |
| Pet-friendly boutique or upscale hotels | $50–$150 per stay | Some offer dog beds and treats. |
| Extended-stay hotels | $75–$200 flat per stay, or $15–$25 per night | Often capped for long stays. |
| Motels | $10–$30 per night | Quality varies. Check reviews carefully. |
| Airbnb or VRBO | $20–$75 per stay, sometimes per night | Hosts set their own fees. Some add a cleaning fee. Always disclose the dog. |
| Rental deposit (Oregon apartment) | $200–$500 refundable, plus $25–$75 monthly pet rent | Landlords can't charge pet fees for service animals or assistance animals. |

**Budget for a typical trip:** 3 road nights at $25–$75 = **about $75–$225**. Add **$75–$200** for temporary housing. Total: roughly **$150–$425**. A few hotel brands waive fees, so it's worth checking.

---

# If You End Up Flying the Dog

Summer is the hardest season to fly a dog. Weigh it carefully.

## Option 1: In the cabin
- **Size limit:** The dog and carrier must fit under the seat. Most airlines cap combined weight at about 20 lb, but it varies. The dog has to be able to stand and turn around.
- **Cost:** About **$95–$150 each way**, plus the airline's carrier requirements.
- **Limits:** Airlines cap the number of pets per flight, so book early. Pets can't sit in exit rows.
- **Paperwork:** Airlines generally want a rabies certificate. Some want a CVI dated within 10 days of travel. Check the specific airline.
- **Prep:** Get the dog used to the carrier for weeks. Book direct flights when possible.

## Option 2: As cargo or checked pet
- **Many major airlines have restricted or stopped this**, so check each one's current policy. Alaska Airlines serves Portland and has handled pets in cargo, but verify.
- **Heat embargoes:** In summer, most airlines refuse checked pets when temperatures at the origin, destination, or any connection exceed a threshold (often about 85°F). A July cross-country flight can easily trigger this.
- **Breed limits:** Flat-faced (brachycephalic) breeds like bulldogs, pugs, and boxers are often banned or restricted because of breathing risks.
- **Cost:** Often **$200–$1,000+**, depending on size and airline.
- **Crate:** It must be airline-approved (IATA-compliant), large enough for the dog to stand and turn, with secure latches and food and water dishes.
- **Paperwork:** A CVI within 10 days of travel is typical, plus a rabies certificate. Some carriers want signed acclimation or live animal forms.

## Option 3: Professional ground pet transport
- A specialist drives your dog cross-country, often in climate-controlled vehicles.
- **Cost:** Roughly **$1,000–$3,000+**, depending on distance and service.
- Vet the company carefully: check licensing, reviews, and how often the dog gets breaks.

## Flying tips
- **Avoid sedation** unless your vet specifically recommends it. Airlines and veterinary groups generally discourage it because of breathing and heart risks at altitude.
- Book early morning or late evening flights in summer.
- Put an ID tag on the dog and the carrier, with your destination address and phone number.
- Carry a photo of the dog, plus the vet records.
- Book pet-friendly lodging at the destination for the arrival night.
- Check **the airline's own page**, since policies change often and sometimes without notice.

**Bottom line:** For a July move, driving the dog with you is usually the safest and cheapest choice. Fly only if the dog is small enough for the cabin or you have a firm reason.

---

# Services and Subscriptions Timeline

**Golden rule:** Never end a service until its replacement is confirmed, and keep a one-day overlap. Take photos of final meter readings.

## T-8 to T-6 weeks (May 21–June 4): Research and book long-lead items
- [ ] **J** **Internet (Oregon):** Book the install now. Installation can take 2+ weeks, and summer moves compete for slots. Ask whether you need to be home. *(HIGH)*
- [ ] **J** **Oregon utilities:** Identify providers by address. Electric is typically PGE or Pacific Power, depending on location. Gas is often NW Natural, and water and trash are usually local or city. Ask about deposits and lead times.
- [ ] **M** **Health insurance:** If you have an employer plan, check network coverage in Oregon. If you buy on the marketplace, a move to a new area generally opens a Special Enrollment Period (usually 60 days), but verify the rules and don't let coverage lapse.
- [ ] **P** **Employer:** Confirm payroll address, state withholding changes (Ohio → Oregon), and benefits.
- [ ] **J** **Gym, lawn service, cleaning service, meal kits:** Check each cancellation notice period. Many gyms require 30 days' written notice.

## T-5 to T-4 weeks (June 11–18): Schedule changes
- [ ] **J** **Ohio utilities (electric, gas, water, trash):** Schedule stop dates for **T+1 day (July 17)**. Ask about final bills and deposit refunds.
- [ ] **J** **Oregon utilities:** Schedule starts for **one or two days before arrival** so power and water are on when you get there. Get confirmation in writing.
- [ ] **M** **Auto insurance:** Call your insurer and ask about Oregon coverage and a new quote. **Don't cancel the old policy until the new one is active.** Oregon requires liability insurance to register.
- [ ] **J** **Renter's or homeowner's insurance:** Cancel the old policy for T+1 and start the new one for the day you get keys.
- [ ] **J** **Prescriptions:** Ask for refills, and transfer them to a national pharmacy chain or an Oregon branch.
- [ ] **J** **Doctor, dentist, and vet records:** Request copies or transfers. Some offices need 1–2 weeks and written forms.

## T-3 weeks (June 25): Notify accounts
- [ ] **J** **Banks and credit cards:** Update the address effective moving day. Ask whether your bank has Oregon branches or good online service.
- [ ] **J** **Loans, student loans, and mortgage servicer:** Update address.
- [ ] **J** **Subscriptions and memberships:** Update billing addresses for streaming, Amazon, and delivery apps. Many keep working but need an address update to avoid failed deliveries.
- [ ] **J** **Employer HR or payroll:** Update address and withholding.
- [ ] **J** **Social Security Administration, IRS (Form 8822), and other federal accounts:** Update your address. You can file Form 8822 or update accounts directly with each agency.

## T-2 weeks (July 2): Cancel and transfer
- [ ] **J** **USPS change of address:** File at usps.com. Set the start date for moving day or the day after. Use the official site only, since lookalike sites charge extra fees.
- [ ] **J** **Cancel or pause:** Gym, lawn service, cable or satellite TV, local newspapers, meal kits, and storage. Return rented equipment such as cable boxes.
- [ ] **J** **Transfer or keep:** Streaming, cloud storage, and phone plans usually travel with you. Check for regional restrictions on streaming.
- [ ] **J** **Phone plan:** Check coverage in your new Oregon area, especially in rural spots.
- [ ] **J** **Toll accounts and parking permits:** Cancel or update (E-ZPass, for example, can often be used in other states, but check).

## T-1 week (July 9): Confirm everything
- [ ] **M** Call Ohio and Oregon utilities to reconfirm dates.
- [ ] **M** Confirm the Oregon internet install date and arrival window.
- [ ] **J** Confirm final bills and where to send them.
- [ ] **J** Download your account statements, since access may be harder after address changes.

## Moving day (July 16)
- [ ] **J** Photograph all utility meters (electric, gas, water) at final walk-through.
- [ ] **J** Return cable boxes, garage openers, and keys.
- [ ] **J** Confirm the forwarding address with the landlord for the deposit refund.

## After arrival (T+1 to T+30)
- [ ] **J** **T+1:** Confirm electric, gas, water, and internet are on and billed to the right names. Photograph the meters at move-in.
- [ ] **J** **T+1:** Renter's or homeowner's insurance active.
- [ ] **J** **T+1 week:** Update voter registration, and check mail forwarding is working.
- [ ] **J** **T+2 weeks:** Update your address with the remaining accounts: loyalty programs, retirement accounts, doctors, subscriptions you missed.
- [ ] **M** **T+2 weeks:** Oregon driver's license and vehicle registration. Update auto insurance to the Oregon address.
- [ ] **J** **T+30 days:** Check that final Ohio bills are paid and deposits returned. Chase anything outstanding.
- [ ] **J** **T+60 days:** Check for stray mail or accounts at the old address, and confirm nothing was missed.

turns.text:
# Budget Totals and Moving-Day One-Pager

**Adjustments to earlier numbers:**
- **Hybrid** now means a portable container (PODS or U-Pack) plus hired loading and unloading labor. The earlier "partial service, $2,500-$5,000" row was too optimistic for 2,400 miles.
- **DMV costs** are widened to $200-$500, since title, registration, and two licenses can exceed my earlier range. Verify at the Oregon DMV site.
- **Meals and tolls** are raised to $300-$500, since $200-$400 was lean for two people over 3-4 days.
- Everything is a 2024-25 ballpark, not live pricing. Summer 2026 prices may be higher, so treat the top of each range as more plausible than the bottom.

**Assumptions:** 2 adults, 1 dog, 1 car, a 1-2 bedroom household, about 2,400 miles. You drive the car and the dog rides with you. Tell me if any of that is wrong and I'll rerun the numbers.

---

# Part 2: Portland DMV and Emissions Steps

Oregon generally wants new residents to register vehicles and get a license within about **30 days**. Verify the current deadline on the Oregon DMV site.

**Order of operations**
1. **Before the move (T-4 weeks):** Call your auto insurer and make sure you'll have coverage from an insurer authorized in Oregon, active by arrival. Oregon DMV checks insurance electronically.
2. **Lien check (T-6 weeks):** If you have a car loan, ask your lienholder how they release or transfer the title to Oregon DMV. This is the most common delay, so start early.
3. **T-2 weeks:** Book DMV appointments online for T+5 to T+14. Portland-area offices fill up, so don't wait until you arrive.
4. **After arrival (T+1 to T+7):** Get the **DEQ emissions test** at a Portland-area Clean Air Station.
   - It's required for most gas vehicles roughly 1975 and newer. Newer vehicles are exempt for their first few model years, and EVs are exempt. Check your model year and fuel type on the DEQ site.
   - Expect about $25-$35 (verify). The passing certificate is time-limited, so don't test too early.
5. **DMV visit (T+5 to T+14):**
   - **License (both of you):** Bring proof of identity (passport or birth certificate), your Social Security number, two proofs of Oregon residency (lease, utility bill), and your Ohio license. A knowledge test is usually waived for a valid out-of-state license (verify). Choose REAL ID if you want it.
   - **Vehicle:** Bring the Ohio title (or lien information), proof of Oregon insurance, the DEQ certificate, and the odometer reading. A VIN verification is usually required for out-of-state vehicles and is done at the DMV or by an authorized provider (verify).
6. **After you get Oregon plates:** Cancel Ohio registration and send back or destroy plates according to Ohio BMV rules.
7. **Dog:** Get a **Multnomah County dog license** (requires rabies proof; usually due within about 30 days of moving). Expect roughly $30-$60/year (verify).
